reasons.detail: Branch treats any 'ses' ending as 'es' plural and strips 'es', so words like 'cases'/'houses'/'horses' (plural of 'case' by adding 's') incorrectly become 'cas'/'hous'/'hors' instead of hitting the final 'strip trailing s' case.

prs.title: fix(snowflake): rewrite COUNT(*) FILTER to COUNT_IF [CLAUDE] (#7900)
prs.taskSummary:
fix(snowflake): rewrite COUNT(*) FILTER to COUNT_IF [CLAUDE] (#7900)

filter_sql rewrites aggregate FILTER into a conditional argument by wrapping
the aggregate's input in IFF(cond, input, NULL). For COUNT(*) that input is a
star, producing COUNT(IFF(cond, *, NULL)) -- a star is not a valid IFF
argument, so Snowflake rejects it.

COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond) counts qualifying rows, which is exactly
Snowflake's native COUNT_IF(cond); emit that instead. Other aggregates and
COUNT(expr)/COUNT(DISTINCT ...) are unaffected.

This completes #7884, which handled the DISTINCT/ORDER BY argument shapes

prs.taskSummary:
fix(postgres)!: default unitless DATEDIFF to DAY instead of AGE [CLAUDE] (#7874)

MySQL DATEDIFF(a, b) parses to a DateDiff node with no unit and always
means a whole-day count. The Postgres generator's _date_diff_sql looked
up DATE_DIFF_FACTOR with an empty unit string, missed the "DAY" entry,
and fell through to the AGE(...) branch. That produced
CAST(AGE(a, b) AS BIGINT), which is invalid Postgres (interval has no
cast to bigint) and semantically wrong (AGE yields a symbolic
year/month/day interval, not a day count).

Default the empty unit to "DAY" before the factor lookup, matching
sqlglo
